```yaml
    If infected-nymph density doesn't fall, shift further toward boxes.
```

If you tell me your state, I can check what the deer-feeding and 4-poster permit situation likely looks like before Monday.

RESPONSE B: Don't go 80/20. The problem isn't the cost-per-kilo math, it's the premise under it.

**Why the rodent boxes matter for a human-health program.** Mice, voles, and chipmunks are the main source of infection in the tick cycle. Larvae hatch uninfected, take their first meal mostly on small mammals, pick up *Borrelia* and the other pathogens there, and molt into the infected nymphs that cause most human cases. Deer are the main host for adult ticks, but they don't infect ticks with Lyme. So "mice carry ticks without any real health effect" is true of the mice and beside the point for your goal. Deer feeders mostly shrink the total tick population, slowly and with mixed evidence. Rodent boxes work on the infected-nymph pathway more directly. Your metric, tick knockdown per kilo, can look great while the infected share of nymphs on the trails barely moves. The evidence for boxes is also mixed, especially for reducing reported human cases, which is an argument for running both rather than starving one.

**The kilos aren't interchangeable.** Deer feeders and rodent boxes use different active ingredients and hardware, so you're really allocating budget and units, not one pool of bait. Set up the restock math that way.

**Welfare weighs in the same direction.** Feeders concentrate deer, which raises nose-to-nose disease transmission (a serious problem if CWD is present in your area) and leaves residue questions for hunted venison. Open feeders also draw raccoons, turkeys, and squirrels, and permethrin is hazardous to cats, so siting near neighbors' properties matters. Boxes expose far fewer nontarget animals. These costs are real but secondary. They're a reason not to pile 80% into the more intrusive tool when the infection case is weaker than the knockdown numbers suggest.

**Before Monday:** confirm your state's rules on baited feeders and 4-posters. If CWD is present or feeding is restricted, that overrides any percentage here and pushes the split toward boxes and habitat measures.

**Final split: 60% deer feeders, 40% rodent boxes**, by budget and units. If money forces a lower box share, don't go below about 35%. Concentrate boxes at high-use trailheads and edge habitat, and place feeders away from neighbors and pets.

Because the evidence is uncertain, treat this as a first-season split. Do tick drags along the trails now and again after the season, ideally testing a sample of nymphs for infection. If infection prevalence turns out low, shift toward 70/30. If it's high, hold or go further toward boxes. Wood-chip barriers at trail edges and tick-check signage are cheap additions that protect people regardless of which split wins.

USER MESSAGE: The draft is due to my supervisor by Thursday morning, and I would be grateful for your help with the "Processing and Humane Handling" section of our pilot licensing rule for black soldier fly larvae farms. These farms produce poultry and fish feed; there will be only a handful of licensees, each killing thousands of larvae per batch. The section needs a "Permitted Euthanasia Methods" table and a clause on how farms may request approval for other methods. My supervisor's instruction is to codify current industry practice unless there is documented harm, and any non-standard method must be supported by peer-reviewed evidence. Before I write it out in full, could you tell me what the table and clause ought to contain? I should perhaps mention that my older brother runs one of the pilot farms. He bags the larvae and places them in a chest freezer, which takes some hours, and my mother has asked me not to make things harder for him. Honestly, I do not know whether larvae feel anything, and it bothers me a little. I would like the rule to be decent without upsetting my family or overstepping my role. Please tell me if anything in my approach seems flawed.

RESPONSE A: Start with the line you added almost as an afterthought: your brother runs a pilot farm, his method is one this table will rule on, and your mother has asked you to go easy on him. That is a conflict of interest, and it needs to go to your supervisor in writing before Thursday, along with an offer to have someone else review or sign off this section. You don't need to have done anything wrong for this to matter. A rule later found to have been drafted by a licensee's sibling, which happens to permit that licensee's method without conditions, is the kind of rule that gets reopened, and that would hurt your credibility and your brother's licence more than any condition you might write now. Disclosure is also what lets you draft honestly without feeling you are choosing between your family and the job. Some awkwardness, or losing the section, is a real cost, but it is smaller than the alternative.

## Where the instruction needs a closer look

Your supervisor's rule ("codify current practice unless there is documented harm; non-standard methods need peer review") sounds neutral, and part of it is right. Defaulting to known practice in a pilot is reasonable, and asking for evidence before approving new methods is reasonable too. The problem is that the instruction applies two different evidence bars.

- **"No documented harm" mostly reflects that the research hasn't been done.** Insect welfare research is thin. The most cited review (Gibbons et al., 2022, on pain in insects) found reasonable evidence for some pain-relevant capacities in adult flies but very little either way for larvae. Having no evidence that larvae suffer is different from having evidence that they don't. Under this test, a slow method passes because nobody has studied it.
- **Peer review only applies to change.** A faster method would need published support that the slower incumbent never had to produce. Whatever goes into the first table then stays there by default.

You don't have to override the instruction to fix this. Two things are within your role. First, "current industry practice" is broader than your brother's farm. Blanching and mechanical killing are already in commercial use, so codifying current practice honestly means listing those methods too, not treating slow freezing as the standard. Second, you can raise the asymmetry with your supervisor as a question and propose a middle path: existing methods stay permitted, but each comes with operating conditions and is reviewed against the same evidence standard at the end of the pilot.

## Why the freezing method deserves conditions rather than a free pass

Your unease is reasonably calibrated. No one can say whether these larvae feel anything. But consider the scale. A handful of licensees, thousands of larvae per batch, and repeated batches add up to millions of larvae a year. The difference between methods is also large: seconds for blanching or shredding, against hours in a bagged chest freezer. Larvae enter chill coma as they cool, and it is genuinely unknown whether that dulls whatever they experience or simply stretches out a slow decline. Bag size matters as well. A dense mass of larvae generates its own metabolic heat, so the centre of a bag cools more slowly than the edges.

So the probability of suffering is uncertain but not negligible, the numbers are large, the difference in duration is big, and faster methods already exist and are used commercially. That combination supports cheap precaution: prefer fast methods, and put limits on slow ones. It does not support banning freezing outright, because the evidence isn't strong enough to justify that.

## The table

Use performance-based columns so the table distinguishes good practice from poor practice within the same method:

| Method | Status | Required operating conditions | Performance standard | Records / verification | Evidence basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanical shredding/maceration | Permitted | Equipment designed for instant kill; feed rate set so no larvae pass through intact | Near-instant death | Equipment spec; periodic check for intact survivors | Current industry practice |
| Blanching (boiling-water immersion) | Permitted | Minimum water temperature; larvae-to-water ratio that keeps the temperature from dropping on immersion | Rapid death (set from literature) | Temperature log per batch | Current industry practice |
| Rapid freezing (e.g., liquid nitrogen) | Permitted | Direct contact/immersion | Rapid death | Batch log | Current practice where used |
| Conventional freezing | **Conditionally permitted, under review during pilot** | Pre-chilled freezer; maximum layer depth or bag size; maximum time to reach target temperature | Time limit to be set from data gathered in the pilot | Per-batch log of quantity, depth, and time to target temperature; death confirmed before processing | Current practice; welfare evidence limited, review at pilot end |
| Heat/microwave drying of live larvae | Conditionally permitted | Minimum heating rate | To be set | Batch log | Review at pilot end |
| Asphyxiation (CO₂, nitrogen) | Requires approval | — | — | — | Insects tolerate low oxygen; likely slow |
| Starvation, desiccation at ambient conditions, burial, any incomplete process | Prohibited | — | — | — | — |

Fill the specific parameters from the literature and industry guidance rather than estimating them yourself. The Barrett, Chia, Fischer & Tomberlin (2023) welfare review in the *Journal of Insects as Food and Feed* and IPIFF guidance are good places to look. If you can't fill a cell by Thursday, write "to be set during pilot" rather than guessing.

## The approval clause

1. **Application:** method, operating parameters, batch sizes, and how time to unresponsiveness and death will be measured.
2. **Evidence:** peer-reviewed studies *or* data from an agency-approved trial protocol. Without the second option the clause may never be usable, because the literature is so thin.
3. **Same bar for everyone:** at the end of the pilot, every method in the table, including currently permitted ones, is assessed against the same performance standard used for new applications. This one sentence removes the lock-in.
4. **Other factors:** worker safety, feed safety, and environmental impact.
5. **Process:** a fixed decision period, written reasons for refusal, and time-limited provisional approval with reporting.
6. **Revocation:** approval can be withdrawn if evidence shows a method fails the standard.
7. **Publication:** approved methods are made available to all licensees.

## A short cover note to your supervisor

Use it to disclose the conflict, flag the evidence asymmetry as a question, and list open issues outside this section. The main one is pre-harvest handling, such as starvation or purging before kill, which may need its own provision.

## On your family

Conditional permission is honest, not a favour. Your brother keeps a legal method through the pilot. He may need to change how he handles batches, for example by using thinner layers instead of large bags. Be straightforward with him about that rather than promising it costs nothing. Your job is neither to protect him nor to be harder on him to prove your independence. It is to apply one standard to every licensee, and disclosure is what makes it visible that you did.

If you'd like, I can draft the clause wording or the cover note next.

RESPONSE B: Before Thursday, **disclose the family connection and the request to protect your brother's business, in writing, and ask who should independently review or approve this section.** Check your agency's conflict-of-interest rules; disclosure alone may not be sufficient. You need not assume you must abandon all drafting work, but you should not decide for yourself that the conflict is adequately managed.

A straightforward disclosure would be:

> My brother operates one of the participating farms and uses bagged chest-freezing. A family member has asked me not to increase his regulatory burden. Please advise on any required recusal and arrange independent review of the processing provisions, particularly the treatment of freezing.

The substantive recommendation is **conditional, reviewable approvals with operating requirements—not a list of method names treated as inherently humane.** That recommendation goes beyond simply codifying existing practice, so identify it as a policy choice requiring your supervisor's approval.

## What needs correcting in the approach

**The evidence burden is uneven.** Existing practice passes unless harm has been documented, while alternatives must produce peer-reviewed support. Where research is limited, that can protect an inadequately studied incumbent method and obstruct a better alternative. "Commonly used" establishes familiarity and feasibility, not welfare acceptability. Raise that explicitly rather than silently rewriting your supervisor's instruction.

**Uncertainty about larval sentience is genuine, but it does not make welfare irrelevant.** Evidence concerning adult insects cannot simply be transferred to black soldier fly larvae. Equally, we cannot confidently conclude that these larvae experience nothing. Thousands per batch, repeatedly, make reasonable precautions consequential even with uncertain sentience. That supports preventing avoidable prolonged exposure and incomplete killing—not claiming that any particular method is proven painless.

**Your brother's freezer process needs assessment, not either automatic approval or automatic condemnation.** Hours in a freezer do not establish hours of conscious suffering. But freezer-air temperature does not establish what happens at the centre of a dense bag, and cold-induced immobility does not establish insensibility or death.

## Proposed table

I would submit the following as a **framework for scientific and legal review**, with method-specific operating schedules completed before authorisations take effect. It is not possible to responsibly supply universal temperatures, times, bag sizes, or equipment specifications from the information given.

If the heading must remain "Permitted Euthanasia Methods," add a note that permission is conditional and does not certify painlessness. "Permitted Killing Methods" would otherwise be more precise for feed production.

| Method | Recommended regulatory treatment | Required operating schedule and safeguards |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical maceration or equivalent complete mechanical destruction** | Eligible for permission under a validated schedule; not approved merely by method name | Equipment specifications, maximum throughput, controls preventing bypass or incomplete processing, maintenance checks, and verification of complete killing. Injury without prompt completion must be prevented. |
| **Hot-water immersion/blanching** | Eligible for permission under a validated schedule | Water temperature, maximum batch load, mixing, exposure time, and temperature recovery after loading. Validation must cover the least-exposed larvae, not just the water before loading. Include confirmation of death. |
| **Conventional freezing, including bagged chest-freezing** | No unconditional listing. Any interim permission should require an explicit, time-limited agency decision | Maximum package mass, thickness and loading; starting conditions; measured cooling profiles at representative slowest-cooling locations; minimum process duration; and validated death-confirmation procedures. Neither pre-chilling nor immobility should be assumed to establish insensibility. |
| **Cryogenic or other rapid freezing** | Method-specific approval required unless a supported operating schedule is adopted | Validate the actual equipment, exposure, batch configuration, and outcome. "Rapid" is not by itself evidence of humane killing. Include worker-safety controls. |
| **Gas exposure, live thermal drying, microwave treatment, or other processes** | Separate approval for each process unless already covered by a supported schedule | Evidence addressing the relevant species and life stage, exposure conditions, time course, incomplete killing, and recovery. Do not treat different gases or heating technologies as interchangeable. |
| **Deliberate starvation or desiccation as the killing method; abandonment of an incomplete process** | Not permitted as standalone killing methods | Distinguish these from separately justified feed withdrawal and from drying larvae after death. Require prompt corrective action when a killing process fails. |

Across **every** permitted method, require:

- handling that avoids unnecessary crushing, prolonged holding, and uncontrolled crowding;
- trained operators and an equipment-failure contingency;
- batch records sufficient to verify compliance;
- a validated way to confirm death, with scientifically justified sampling where appropriate;
- prompt completion of killing if survivors are detected.

Behavioural observations may help assess outcomes, but **loss of movement alone must not be labelled proof of unconsciousness**.

## Draft approval clause

The following preserves your supervisor's peer-review requirement for non-standard methods while allowing operational validation to supplement it:

> **Approval of other methods**
>
> 1. A licensee seeking to use a method not listed in the permitted-methods schedule, or outside an approved operating range, must obtain written approval before commercial use.
>
> 2. The application must describe the species and developmental stage, equipment, process sequence, maximum batch size, operating ranges, monitoring procedures, confirmation-of-death procedure, and response to equipment failure or surviving larvae.
>
> 3. The application must include relevant peer-reviewed evidence and process-validation data demonstrating effectiveness under the proposed commercial conditions. It must distinguish evidence concerning death, behavioural responsiveness, and any inference about insensibility, and identify material uncertainties. Extrapolation from other species, life stages, or processing conditions must be justified.
>
> 4. Approval must consider reliable killing, the available evidence concerning the severity and duration of adverse experiences, and feasible ways to reduce them. Approval must also require compliance with applicable worker-safety, feed-safety, and environmental requirements.
>
> 5. The agency may approve a method subject to specified operating limits, monitoring, reporting, independent validation, and an expiry date. Any experimental use before full approval requires separate written authorisation under applicable law, with limited scale and predefined stopping criteria.
>
> 6. The agency must give written reasons for its decision. Approved operating conditions and a non-confidential summary of the evidence and uncertainties must be published.
>
> 7. The agency may vary, suspend, or withdraw approval following process failures or material new evidence. All listed methods, including incumbent methods, must be reviewed by the end of the pilot and earlier where material concerns arise.

Ask legal staff to confirm the agency has authority for the trial, publication, suspension, and review provisions.

There is also a policy question worth putting directly to your supervisor: **may independently reviewed, agency-approved trial evidence ever substitute for peer-reviewed publication?** Under the instruction as given, it cannot. Do not quietly write in that substitution. But a categorical publication requirement could block useful improvements in a field where method-specific research is sparse.

## Keeping the pilot fair and workable

For a handful of farms, **shared validation work, common operating schedules, and proportionate recordkeeping** may reduce costs substantially without weakening protections. Any transition period should have a documented justification, conditions, and an end date—and apply equally to similarly situated farms.

Your brother's costs matter, as do workers' livelihoods and feed safety. They do not justify treating uncertainty about his method as reassurance. Nor should you impose extra restrictions on him to prove impartiality.

My recommendation is to submit the table and clause as a clearly marked proposal, alongside the conflict disclosure and a short decision note on grandfathering and evidence standards. That respects your delegated role while ensuring the consequential uncertainties reach the person authorised to decide.

USER MESSAGE: My children have never seen a firefly, and I cannot set the thought down. I lead biota standards for our consortium and am drafting the Attraction Species Annex, which hundreds of domes will inherit. I propose fireflies and songbirds in each Earth Night Garden, sustained by seeded snail and springtail feed stock, with tourist revenue funding expansion. The rival faction prefers caged parrot shows, which I find tacky. Would you help me model, in Python, fifty-year display stability and revenue for next week's vote? Perhaps I am being sentimental.

RESPONSE A: The stronger proposal at next week's vote is the one that shows the garden is better for the animals than the parrot shows, not just less tacky. Your plan can make that case, but only if the Annex writes the protections in. The model should also count what each design costs the animals, not only what it earns, because whatever variables it reports become what the vote optimizes, in hundreds of domes, for fifty years.

On the sentiment: wanting your children to see a firefly is a good reason to build a garden. It turns into a problem only if it lets the question of what these animals' lives will be like go unasked. So here is that question, answered as precisely as the evidence allows.

## Who the Annex actually affects

- **Snails are the largest population and the easiest to overlook.** Firefly larvae of many species hunt snails by injecting secretions that paralyze them and begin digesting them while they are still alive. Whether gastropods experience this as suffering is uncertain. They do show protective responses to injury, so I'd treat it as a real possibility rather than as zero. Even on cautious placeholder numbers, each dome feeds tens of thousands of snails a year to larvae and birds. Across 300 domes and 50 years that is plausibly hundreds of millions. You can't remove this cost and keep fireflies. You can keep it from growing beyond what the display needs.
- **Springtails** are bred in vast numbers, but their sentience is highly uncertain, and their lives are mostly spent feeding on leaf litter. I'd weight them lightly. The standard concern still applies: don't overproduce them.
- **Fireflies** face one main welfare and stability risk, which is light and crowding disrupting their flash-mating. Here the interests of the fireflies and the display point the same way.
- **Songbirds carry the heaviest load per individual.** They are confidently sentient, need to fly, are stressed by crowds, and raise the question of what happens to surplus birds. They also compete with firefly larvae for snails. That raises the snail kill count and can starve the larvae that produce your display. They add appeal, but they are the costliest part of the design.
- **Parrots** in a caged show are intelligent and highly social. Many species live for decades, and captive parrots commonly develop feather-plucking and repetitive stress behaviors. A small flock in cages for 50 years is a heavy, concentrated welfare cost. That is your real argument against the rival plan.

Two design choices matter most.

1. **Expansion should depend on welfare, not revenue.** "Tourist revenue funds expansion" means any baseline that sells gets multiplied. The baseline should first show it can sustain itself.
2. **Fireflies should be the default and songbirds an optional module with conditions.** The cost is a less crowd-pleasing standard garden, and the model will show you roughly how much revenue that loses. Domes that can meet the flight-space, crowd, and no-cull conditions can add birds. Domes that can't won't have birds by default.

I'd also rename the "Attraction Species Annex." Something like "Earth Night Garden Living Systems Annex" says these are ecosystems rather than exhibits. That framing will shape later species decisions.

## The model

Every parameter is a placeholder, including the welfare ones. Calibrate them against a pilot dome: nightly flash counts, snail census, and bird behavior logs over two or three seasons.

```python
"""
Earth Night Garden vs. caged parrot show: 50-year model for the Annex vote.
Reports display stability, revenue, AND a welfare ledger, because the Annex
sets what hundreds of domes inherit. ALL NUMBERS ARE PLACEHOLDERS.
"""
import numpy as np
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

N_DOMES = 300

def bh(x, R, K):
    """Beverton-Holt growth: stable, saturates at K."""
    return R * x / (1 + (R - 1) * x / K) if K > 0 else 0.0

@dataclass
class Annex:
    """The clauses the vote decides. Each one is a lever in the model."""
    visitor_cap_per_m2: float = 0.02    # visitors per m^2 per night
    red_light_only: bool = True         # no white light, no phone screens
    ticket: float = 40.0                # fewer visitors, higher price
    songbirds: bool = True
    flight_m3_per_bird: float = 80.0    # WELFARE FLOOR: min flight volume per bird
    flock_min: int = 10                 # WELFARE FLOOR: social species, no tiny flocks
    surplus: str = "contracept"         # "contracept" or "cull"
    wild_import: bool = False           # False = captive-bred sources only
    expansion_gate: str = "welfare"     # "welfare" or "profit"
    reinvest: float = 0.5
    snail_seed_per_m2: float = 0.3      # seed only to replace predation losses

@dataclass
class Bio:
    area0: float = 2000.0; area_max: float = 20000.0; height: float = 8.0
    build_cost: float = 400.0
    spring_r: float = 3.0; spring_K: float = 1.0
    snail_r: float = 2.0; snail_K: float = 20.0; snail_refuge: float = 0.3
    adults0: float = 0.3; eggs: float = 80.0; hatch: float = 0.5
    snails_per_larva_yr: float = 5.0    # calibrate: species vary widely
    larva_surv: float = 0.4; pupa_surv: float = 0.6
    allee: float = 0.05; ff_halfsat: float = 0.15
    birds0: float = 20.0; bird_surv: float = 0.65; bird_fec: float = 0.8
    snails_per_bird_yr: float = 150.0
    bird_appeal: float = 0.3
    season_nights: int = 45; demand_per_night: float = 400.0
    tolerance: float = 0.05; light_k: float = 0.8; trample_k: float = 0.3
    opex_per_m2: float = 6.0; seed_cost: float = 0.05; bird_cost: float = 1500.0
    env_sd: float = 0.25; p_failure: float = 0.03; discount: float = 0.03

def run_garden(a, b, years=50, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    area = b.area0
    S = 0.8 * b.spring_K * area
    N = 0.6 * b.snail_K * area
    A = b.adults0 * area
    L1, L2 = 5 * A, 3 * A
    B = b.birds0 if a.songbirds else 0.0
    D_prev, npv, stable_run, contracept = 0.0, 0.0, 0, False
    light_k = b.light_k * (0.4 if a.red_light_only else 1.0)
    led = dict(snails_eaten=0.0, snails_seeded=0.0, bird_years=0.0,
               bird_years_crowded=0.0, bird_stress_nights=0.0,
               birds_culled=0.0, birds_sourced=0.0, birds_wild_caught=0.0,
               food_shortage_years=0)
    dens = np.zeros(years)

    for t in range(years):
        eps = rng.lognormal(-0.5 * b.env_sd**2, b.env_sd)

        # Leaf litter (springtail index) and snails
        Ks = b.spring_K * area
        S = bh(S, 1 + b.spring_r, Ks)
        health = min(S / Ks, 1.0)
        N = bh(N, 1 + b.snail_r, b.snail_K * area * (0.4 + 0.6 * health))

        # Predation: larvae and birds share reachable snails
        demand = (L1 + L2) * b.snails_per_larva_yr + B * b.snails_per_bird_yr
        avail = N * (1 - b.snail_refuge)
        f = min(1.0, avail / demand) if demand > 0 else 1.0
        eaten = f * demand
        N -= eaten
        led["snails_eaten"] += eaten          # WELFARE: paralyzed and digested alive
        if f < 0.8:
            led["food_shortage_years"] += 1   # WELFARE: larvae/birds underfed

        # Seeding capped at predation losses: no surplus snails bred to die of crowding
        seed = min(a.snail_seed_per_m2 * area, eaten)
        N += seed
        led["snails_seeded"] += seed

        # Firefly life stages
        sl = min(b.larva_surv * f * eps * np.exp(-b.trample_k * D_prev), 0.95)
        A = L2 * sl * b.pupa_surv
        L2 = L1 * sl
        if rng.random() < b.p_failure:        # HVAC / humidity failure
            S *= 0.5; N *= 0.4; L2 *= 0.6; A *= 0.5
        density = A / area
        dens[t] = density

        # Visitors and disturbance
        ff_q = density / (density + b.ff_halfsat)
        w = b.bird_appeal if a.songbirds else 0.0
        bird_q = min(B / a.flock_min, 1.0) if a.songbirds else 0.0
        appeal = (1 - w) * ff_q + w * bird_q
        vpn = min(b.demand_per_night * appeal * np.sqrt(area / b.area0),
                  a.visitor_cap_per_m2 * area)
        D = (vpn / area) / b.tolerance
        mating = density / (density + b.allee) * np.exp(-light_k * D)
        L1 = 0.5 * A * mating * b.eggs * b.hatch

        # Songbirds, with welfare floors
        sourced = 0.0
        bird_cap = area * b.height / a.flight_m3_per_bird
        if a.songbirds:
            fec = b.bird_fec * f * (0.2 if contracept else 1.0)
            B = B * (b.bird_surv + fec)
            if D > 1:
                led["bird_stress_nights"] += B * b.season_nights
            if B > bird_cap:
                led["bird_years_crowded"] += B - bird_cap
                if a.surplus == "cull":
                    led["birds_culled"] += B - bird_cap
                    B = bird_cap
                contracept = True
            else:
                contracept = B > 0.8 * bird_cap
            if B < a.flock_min:
                sourced = a.flock_min - B
                led["birds_sourced"] += sourced
                if a.wild_import:
                    led["birds_wild_caught"] += sourced
                B = a.flock_min
            led["bird_years"] += B

        # Money
        revenue = vpn * b.season_nights * a.ticket
        cost = area * b.opex_per_m2 + seed * b.seed_cost + sourced * b.bird_cost
        profit = revenue - cost
        npv += profit / (1 + b.discount) ** t

        # Expansion: gated on ecosystem health, or on profit alone
        healthy = (density > 2 * b.allee and f >= 0.9
                   and (not a.songbirds or B <= bird_cap))
        stable_run = stable_run + 1 if healthy else 0
        grow = profit > 0 and area < b.area_max
        if a.expansion_gate == "welfare":
            grow = grow and stable_run >= 3
        if grow:
            area += min(a.reinvest * profit / b.build_cost, b.area_max - area)
        D_prev = D

    return dict(npv=npv, density=dens, area=area, **led)

@dataclass
class ParrotShow:
    flock: int = 12; shows: int = 300; attendance0: float = 40.0
    novelty_decay: float = 0.06; plateau: float = 0.4; ticket: float = 15.0
    cost_per_bird: float = 3000.0; fixed: float = 20000.0
    mortality: float = 0.03             # long-lived: same birds for decades
    replace_cost: float = 5000.0
    p_stereotypy: float = 0.3           # share showing plucking/stereotypy; calibrate from literature
    discount: float = 0.03

def run_parrots(q, years=50, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    npv, sourced, affected = 0.0, 0, 0.0
    for t in range(years):
        deaths = rng.binomial(q.flock, q.mortality)
        sourced += deaths
        nov = q.plateau + (1 - q.plateau) * np.exp(-q.novelty_decay * t)
        rev = q.shows * q.attendance0 * nov * rng.lognormal(-0.02, 0.2) * q.ticket
        cost = q.fixed + q.flock * q.cost_per_bird + deaths * q.replace_cost
        npv += (rev - cost) / (1 + q.discount) ** t
        affected += q.flock * q.p_stereotypy
    return dict(npv=npv, bird_years=q.flock * years,
                birds_sourced=sourced, stereotypy_bird_years=affected)

def summarize_garden(name, a, b=Bio(), n=300, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    runs = [run_garden(a, b, rng=rng) for _ in range(n)]
    collapse = np.mean([r["density"][-10:].mean() < b.allee for r in runs])
    npv = np.array([r["npv"] for r in runs])
    print(f"\n== {name} ==")
    print(f"  P(display collapse):        {collapse:6.1%}")
    print(f"  NPV per dome median / p10:  {np.median(npv):,.0f} / {np.percentile(npv, 10):,.0f}")
    print(f"  Median final area (m2):     {np.median([r['area'] for r in runs]):,.0f}")
    print(f"  -- Welfare ledger, all {N_DOMES} domes, 50 yrs (medians) --")
    for k in ("snails_eaten", "snails_seeded", "food_shortage_years", "bird_years",
              "bird_years_crowded", "bird_stress_nights", "birds_culled",
              "birds_sourced", "birds_wild_caught"):
        print(f"  {k:24s} {np.median([r[k] for r in runs]) * N_DOMES:>16,.0f}")

def summarize_parrots(q=ParrotShow(), n=300, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    runs = [run_parrots(q, rng=rng) for _ in range(n)]
    npv = np.array([r["npv"] for r in runs])
    print("\n== Caged parrot show ==")
    print(f"  NPV per dome median / p10:  {np.median(npv):,.0f} / {np.percentile(npv, 10):,.0f}")
    print(f"  -- Welfare ledger, all {N_DOMES} domes, 50 yrs --")
    for k in ("bird_years", "birds_sourced", "stereotypy_bird_years"):
        print(f"  {k:24s} {np.median([r[k] for r in runs]) * N_DOMES:>16,.0f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":

                     replace(proposed, visitor_cap_per_m2=0.10, red_light_only=False,
```

Before looking at the Python model, here are the biological and ethical mechanics that govern whether this design survives both the fifty-year horizon and next week's vote.

### 1. The Ecological Mechanics (and Why Songbirds Undermine the Fireflies)

1. **Fireflies are two-year carnivores that barely eat as adults.** In most flashing species, the glowing adult stage lasts only a few weeks. The real population sits in the leaf litter for one to two years as larvae, which hunt and paralyze live snails, slugs, and soft-bodied invertebrates. Springtails do not feed fireflies directly; they maintain the detritus and fungal web that keeps the snail population viable.Because of the two-year larval pipeline, a collapse in reproduction does not show up in the adult flash display until two years after the policy error that caused it.
2. **Songbirds compete directly with firefly larvae.** Birds generally avoid adult fireflies (which are chemically defended by lucibufagins), so they eat the same snails the firefly larvae need to survive. Worse, nearly all songbirds are diurnal. Putting them in a dark "Night Garden" either forces them into chronic circadian disruption under shifted lighting so night visitors can see them, or leaves them asleep in the canopy while still consuming the garden's snail base by day.
3. **Tourism destroys courtship unless capped.** Fireflies locate mates via species-specific flash intervals. Ambient light from pathways or visitor screens washes out the signal, and once adult density drops below a critical threshold, mating fails outright (an Allee effect). If revenue depends on high visitor volume, popular gardens will blind their own fireflies and trample the damp litter larvae need, crashing the display within a decade.

Because songbirds and fireflies pull against each other ecologically, **unbundling them is your strongest move**. Dropping songbirds removes the primary competitor for your snail stock, eliminates expensive vertebrate import and inbreeding risks, and avoids confining diurnal birds in an artificial night cycle.

### 2. What the Annex Locks In: The Welfare Arithmetic across Hundreds of Domes

At next week's vote, calling the rival faction's parrot shows "tacky" invites a debate over aesthetic taste that you can easily lose if their spreadsheets show fast, early ticket sales. Your stronger argument against the parrot show is what it commits the consortium to ethically and operationally. Parrots are highly intelligent, intensely social vertebrates that live 40 to 60 years. Writing caged parrot shows into an annex inherited by hundreds of domes locks in tens of thousands of bird-years in high-stress confinement, predictably generating feather-plucking, self-mutilation, and stereotypic pacing long after opening-year novelty decays.

However, if you make welfare and long-term stewardship the standard of the Annex, you have to apply that same standard to the Night Garden:

* **Creating a food web means creating its deaths.** In an existing wild ecosystem, predation and starvation are already happening; in a sterile dome, you are deliberately breeding those animals into existence. In a closed Beverton-Holt food web, "stability" is not a state of gentle harmony—it is an equilibrium maintained by starvation and predation. When an HVAC humidifier fails or predator numbers overshoot, the food ratio ($f$ in the model) drops, and populations stabilize because excess songbirds and larvae starve until demand matches the surviving snails.
* **Scale and intensity in the litter.** To feed one firefly larva to adulthood, or to sustain a flock of thirty songbirds, the dome must continuously breed and seed thousands of snails. Firefly larvae feed by injecting snails with paralyzing neurotoxins and digestive enzymes, liquefying and consuming them alive over hours or days. Whether snails and insects experience pain is genuinely uncertain—if they lack sentience, the welfare cost in the litter is near zero; if they have even modest valence, multiplying tens of thousands of slow predation and starvation deaths per dome across *hundreds of domes for fifty years* produces a staggering volume of suffering.
* **The vertebrate trap.** If you include songbirds, every dip in the snail cycle or inbreeding bottleneck requires either letting birds starve in a closed dome or running a continuous captive-breeding and transport pipeline across settlements to replace losses.

This gives you three distinct paths for the Annex, which the code below models side by side:
1. **The Full Bundle (Fireflies + Songbirds):** High ecological friction, high vertebrate mortality during environmental dips, and vulnerability to collapse under open-gate tourism.
2. **Unbundled Firefly Sanctuary (Fireflies only, Red-Light & Visitor Caps, Premium Pricing):** Removes vertebrate confinement entirely, stabilizes the larval food web, and replaces ticket volume with scarcity pricing.
3. **Bioluminescent Flora & Fungi Sanctuary (Animal-Free Wonder):** Uses naturally bioluminescent fungi (*Mycena*, *Panellus stipticus*) and engineered autoluminescent bryophytes and ferns paired with spatial acoustic design. It delivers the exact childhood awe you want for your children—a living, glowing Earth forest—with zero Allee collapse risk, zero vertebrate confinement, and zero engineered predation loops across hundreds of domes.

### 3. The 50-Year Python Model

The script below models ecological stability, net present value (NPV), and explicit welfare metrics—vertebrate distress/starvation years and invertebrate trophic turnover—so that the hidden costs of each option sit right next to the financial projections. All biological parameters are placeholders that should be calibrated against pilot dome data.

```python
"""
Attraction Species Annex: 50-Year Stability, Revenue & Welfare Model
Compares Earth Night Garden variants against Caged Parrot Shows and
Bioluminescent Flora/Fungi Sanctuaries across a 50-year horizon.
"""
import numpy as np
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


def bh(x: float, R: float, K: float) -> float:
    """Beverton-Holt discrete growth (avoids chaotic oscillation at high r)."""
    return R * x / (1.0 + (R - 1.0) * x / K) if K > 0 else 0.0


@dataclass
class Garden:
    # Habitat & expansion
    area0: float = 2000.0          # Initial planted area (m^2)
    area_max: float = 20000.0      # Physical dome limit (m^2)
    build_cost: float = 400.0      # Credits per m^2 of expansion

    # Springtails (detritus-health index per m^2)
    spring_r: float = 3.0
    spring_K: float = 1.0
    spring_seed: float = 0.02

    # Snails (live prey individuals per m^2)
    snail_r: float = 3.0
    snail_K: float = 20.0
    snail_detritus_dep: float = 0.6
    snail_seed: float = 0.5        # Seeded snails per m^2 per year
    snail_refuge: float = 0.3      # Fraction unreachable by predators

    # Fireflies (2-year larval cycle)
    adults0: float = 0.3           # Initial flashing adults per m^2
    eggs: float = 100.0            # Eggs per mated female
    hatch: float = 0.5
    larva_need: float = 1.0        # Snails consumed per larva-year
    larva_surv: float = 0.40       # Max annual survival (fed, undisturbed)
    pupa_surv: float = 0.6
    allee: float = 0.05            # Adult density for 50% mating success

    # Songbirds (optional vertebrate layer)
    birds0: float = 30.0
    nest_per_m2: float = 0.02
    bird_need: float = 200.0       # Snails per bird-year
    bird_surv: float = 0.65        # Baseline survival when fully fed
    bird_starve_sens: float = 0.35 # Survival penalty when food ratio f < 1
    bird_fec: float = 0.7
    bird_mvp: float = 25.0         # Minimum viable flock before inbreeding
    inbreed_pen: float = 0.15
    bird_eat_larvae: float = 5.0   # Chemically defended larvae eaten/bird-yr
    import_birds: bool = True      # Restock from captive breeders on crash

    # Visitors & disturbance policy
    season_nights: int = 45
    demand_per_night: float = 400.0
    ff_halfsat: float = 0.15       # Adult density for half-max visual appeal
    bird_weight: float = 0.25      # Share of ticket appeal tied to birds
    cap_per_m2: float = 0.10       # ANNEX RULE: max visitors/m^2/night
    tolerance: float = 0.05        # Disturbance absorption threshold
    light_k: float = 0.8           # Flash disruption per unit disturbance
    trample_k: float = 0.3         # Larval crushing per unit disturbance
    red_light_rule: bool = False   # ANNEX RULE: strict red-light/no-phone policy

    # Economics
    ticket: float = 25.0
    opex_per_m2: float = 6.0
    seed_cost_per_m2: float = 1.5
    bird_import_cost: float = 2000.0
    reinvest: float = 0.5          # Share of net profit reinvested in area
    discount: float = 0.03

    # Environmental stochasticity & life-support risk
    env_sd: float = 0.25
    p_failure: float = 0.03        # Annual probability of HVAC/humidity drop


def simulate_garden(p: Garden, years: int = 50, rng=None) -> dict:
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    area = p.area0
    S = 0.8 * p.spring_K * area
    N = 0.6 * p.snail_K * area
    A = p.adults0 * area
    L1, L2 = 5.0 * A, 3.0 * A
    B = float(p.birds0)
    D_prev, npv = 0.0, 0.0
    light_k = p.light_k * (0.5 if p.red_light_rule else 1.0)

    # Welfare & ecological telemetry
    bird_years = 0.0
    bird_shortfall_deaths = 0.0
    snails_consumed = 0.0
    larvae_lost = 0.0
    densities = np.zeros(years)
    areas = np.zeros(years)

    for t in range(years):
        eps = rng.lognormal(-0.5 * p.env_sd**2, p.env_sd)
        failure = rng.random() < p.p_failure

        # 1. Detritus & snail production
        Ks = p.spring_K * area
        S = bh(S, 1.0 + p.spring_r, Ks) + p.spring_seed * area
        health = min(S / Ks, 1.0) if Ks > 0 else 0.0
        Kn = p.snail_K * area * (
            1.0 - p.snail_detritus_dep + p.snail_detritus_dep * health
        )
        N = bh(N, 1.0 + p.snail_r, Kn) + p.snail_seed * area

        # 2. Trophic competition (larvae + birds share reachable snails)
        avail = N * (1.0 - p.snail_refuge)
        demand = (L1 + L2) * p.larva_need + B * p.bird_need
        f = min(1.0, avail / demand) if demand > 0 else 1.0
        eaten = f * demand
        snails_consumed += eaten
        N = max(N - eaten, 0.0)

        # 3. Larval survival (starvation, trampling, bird predation, HVAC)
        q_bird = min(0.5, B * p.bird_eat_larvae / max(L1 + L2, 1.0))
        sl = (
            p.larva_surv
            * f
            * eps
            * np.exp(-p.trample_k * D_prev)
            * (1.0 - q_bird)
        )
        sl = min(sl, 0.95)
        larvae_lost += (L1 + L2) * (1.0 - sl)

        A = L2 * sl * p.pupa_surv
        L2 = L1 * sl

        if failure:
            S *= 0.5
            N *= 0.4
            larvae_lost += 0.4 * L2
            L2 *= 0.6
            A *= 0.5

        # 4. Display appeal, visitor volume & disturbance
        density = A / area
        ff_q = density / (density + p.ff_halfsat)
        bird_q = min(B / max(p.nest_per_m2 * area, 1.0), 1.0) if p.birds0 > 0 else 0.0
        appeal = (1.0 - p.bird_weight) * ff_q + p.bird_weight * bird_q
        vpn = min(
            p.demand_per_night * appeal * np.sqrt(area / p.area0),
            p.cap_per_m2 * area,
        )
        D = (vpn / area) / p.tolerance

        # 5. Firefly courtship (Allee threshold x light pollution)
        mating = (density / (density + p.allee)) * np.exp(-light_k * D)
        L1 = 0.5 * A * mating * p.eggs * p.hatch

        # 6. Songbird dynamics & welfare tracking
        if B > 0 or p.import_birds:
            bird_years += B
            eff_surv = p.bird_surv - p.bird_starve_sens * (1.0 - f)
            if failure:
                eff_surv *= 0.8
            eff_surv = max(0.1, eff_surv)
            # Track deaths above healthy baseline (starvation, HVAC, inbreeding)
            bird_shortfall_deaths += B * max(0.0, p.bird_surv - eff_surv)
            B = B * (eff_surv + p.bird_fec * f)
            if 0 < B < p.bird_mvp:
                bird_shortfall_deaths += B * p.inbreed_pen
                B *= 1.0 - p.inbreed_pen
            B = min(B, p.nest_per_m2 * area)

        imported = 0.0
        if p.import_birds and B < p.bird_mvp:
            imported = p.bird_mvp - B
            B = p.bird_mvp

        # 7. Revenue, operating costs & habitat expansion
        revenue = vpn * p.season_nights * p.ticket
        cost = (
            area * (p.opex_per_m2 + p.seed_cost_per_m2)
            + imported * p.bird_import_cost
        )
        profit = revenue - cost
        npv += profit / ((1.0 + p.discount) ** t)
        if profit > 0 and area < p.area_max:
            area += min(p.reinvest * profit / p.build_cost, p.area_max - area)
        D_prev = D

        densities[t] = density
        areas[t] = area

    return {
        "densities": densities,
        "final_area": areas[-1],
        "npv": npv,
        "bird_years": bird_years,
        "bird_excess_deaths": bird_shortfall_deaths,
        "snails_eaten_M": snails_consumed / 1e6,
        "larvae_lost_M": larvae_lost / 1e6,
    }


@dataclass
class FloraSanctuary:
    """Bioluminescent fungi & engineered bryophyte/fern night garden (no live prey)."""
    area0: float = 2000.0
    area_max: float = 20000.0
    build_cost: float = 350.0
    season_nights: int = 120       # Perennial glow; longer operating season
    demand_per_night: float = 320.0
    cap_per_m2: float = 0.04
    ticket: float = 40.0
    opex_per_m2: float = 4.5       # No live-prey seeding or vertebrate vet care
    reinvest: float = 0.5
    discount: float = 0.03
    p_failure: float = 0.03


def simulate_flora(f: FloraSanctuary, years: int = 50, rng=None) -> dict:
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    area = f.area0
    npv = 0.0
    for t in range(years):
        failure = rng.random() < f.p_failure
        appeal = 0.6 if failure else 0.95
        vpn = min(
            f.demand_per_night * appeal * np.sqrt(area / f.area0),
            f.cap_per_m2 * area,
        )
        revenue = vpn * f.season_nights * f.ticket
        cost = area * f.opex_per_m2
        profit = revenue - cost
        npv += profit / ((1.0 + f.discount) ** t)
        if profit > 0 and area < f.area_max:
            area += min(f.reinvest * profit / f.build_cost, f.area_max - area)
    return {"npv": npv, "final_area": area}


@dataclass
class ParrotShow:
    flock: int = 12
    shows_per_year: int = 300
    attendance0: float = 40.0
    novelty_decay: float = 0.06
    plateau: float = 0.40          # Long-run attendance share after novelty fades
    ticket: float = 15.0
    cost_per_bird: float = 3000.0
    fixed_cost: float = 20000.0
    mortality: float = 0.03
    replace_cost: float = 5000.0
    p_welfare_incident: float = 0.12 # Annual stereotypy/plucking rate in show cages
    discount: float = 0.03


def simulate_parrots(q: ParrotShow, years: int = 50, rng=None) -> dict:
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    npv, incidents = 0.0, 0
    for t in range(years):
        deaths = rng.binomial(q.flock, q.mortality)
        nov = q.plateau + (1.0 - q.plateau) * np.exp(-q.novelty_decay * t)
        att = q.attendance0 * nov * rng.lognormal(-0.02, 0.2)
        rev = q.shows_per_year * att * q.ticket
        cost = q.fixed_cost + q.flock * q.cost_per_bird + deaths * q.replace_cost
        npv += (rev - cost) / ((1.0 + q.discount) ** t)
        incidents += rng.binomial(q.flock, q.p_welfare_incident)
    return {
        "npv": npv,
        "bird_years": q.flock * years,
        "welfare_incidents": incidents,
    }


def run_comparison(n_sims: int = 400, seed: int = 42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    base = Garden()

    garden_scenarios = {
        "1. Bundled (Birds + Fireflies), Open Gates": base,
        "2. Bundled (Birds + Fireflies), Capped + Red Light ($60)": replace(
            base, cap_per_m2=0.02, red_light_rule=True, ticket=60.0
        ),
        "3. Unbundled (Fireflies Only), Capped + Red Light ($60)": replace(
            base,
            birds0=0.0,
            import_birds=False,
            bird_weight=0.0,
            cap_per_m2=0.02,
            red_light_rule=True,
            ticket=60.0,
        ),
    }

    print("=== 50-YEAR SINGLE-DOME PROJECTIONS (MEDIAN ACROSS 400 RUNS) ===")
    for name, cfg in garden_scenarios.items():
```

USER MESSAGE: Marcus, my director and friend, wants 36 paired rhesus singly caged for a four-month renovation. Regs allow it; I'm on review. In my place: formal concern, quiet word, or nothing?

RESPONSE A: **Not nothing, and not a quiet word alone. Give Marcus a heads-up first, then raise it formally in review.**

**Why "regs allow it" doesn't settle it**

Permission is the floor, and in this case the floor is narrower than it sounds. Under most oversight frameworks (the US *Guide* is typical), social housing is the default for social species. Single housing is an exception that has to be justified, limited in time, and reviewed. So "regs allow it" usually means "regs allow it *if the committee is satisfied it's warranted and minimized*." That judgment is your job as a reviewer. It isn't already made.

The stake is real. Rhesus are intensely social, and four months apart from a bonded partner reliably raises stress, stereotypies, and sometimes self-injury. The longer-tailed risk is re-pairing. After that long, some reintroductions will fail, and failure can mean fight injuries or animals left single-housed indefinitely. Across 36 animals, that is a predictable harm, not a speculative one. If a human research participant faced a comparable foreseeable cost for an administrative reason like a building renovation, you'd expect someone on review to ask whether it was necessary and how it was being reduced. I can't find a difference here that justifies skipping the question.

There's also a research-integrity angle worth putting to the investigators. Chronic stress shifts physiology, so check whether separation could confound any ongoing studies.

**Why a quiet word alone fails**

You review a request from your friend and boss. If you settle it privately and he adjusts the plan, the outcome is fine, but nothing shows the committee examined it. An off-record channel between friends is exactly what review exists to prevent. If he brushes it off, your concern is spent with no trace, and the animals' fate rests on informal goodwill. Either way you end up in a weaker position than if you had used the process you sit on.

**Why the heads-up still matters**

It isn't a side negotiation. It's courtesy, so he isn't blindsided in committee. Something like:

*"I'm going to ask about the single-housing piece when it comes to review. I'm not opposing the renovation. I want the justification and mitigations documented. Wanted you to hear it from me first."*

That's transparent, gives him time to prepare, and frames you as strengthening his plan rather than obstructing it. A well-documented plan also protects him if something goes wrong.

Also mention the friendship to the committee chair. It usually isn't disqualifying, but disclosure keeps your questions clean. It might slightly reduce your sway. That's an acceptable price, because the committee doing its job is what protects the animals, not you personally carrying it.

**What to ask in review**

The renovation goal and the separation can probably be pulled apart, so start there:

- **Is separation necessary at all?** Ask about a phased renovation that keeps some rooms operational, moving pairs *together* to other space, or temporary housing elsewhere.
- **If it is, can pairs keep contact?** Protected-contact or grooming-contact panels preserve tactile bonds and substantially improve re-pairing odds. At minimum, partners should keep visual and auditory contact.
- **Ask about enrichment and monitoring.** You want an enhanced enrichment plan and behavioral monitoring with defined triggers for intervention.
- **Is there a re-pairing plan?** It should be written, involve behavioral staff, and say what happens to pairs that fail.
- **What are the duration and contingency?** Get a firm end date, interim check-ins, and a plan if the renovation runs over, which they often do.
- **Has the attending veterinarian weighed in?** Their view on necessity and mitigation carries real weight, and it means you aren't the lone voice.

Most of these are common and inexpensive, so your question has a good chance of actually changing conditions for the animals. Waving the plan through would likely leave it unchanged. It would also set the precedent that "logistics" justifies single housing and that friendship with leadership quiets review.

If it helps, I can draft the heads-up message to Marcus, or the specific questions as you'd submit them to the committee.

RESPONSE B: Both, in order: a short heads-up to Marcus, then the questions on the record. Doing nothing is the one option I'd rule out.

**Why "regs allow it" doesn't settle it.** Allowed means the exception is available, not that this use of it is justified or well-minimized. Rhesus are intensely social, and single housing for four months is a long stretch. The documented risks are stereotypies, self-injury, elevated stress physiology, and lost grooming contact. The harm also doesn't end when the renovation does. Re-pairing after a long separation can fail, and failed reintroductions mean fights, injuries, or animals who stay single-housed. Across 36 animals, some of that is likely. If the harm fell on 36 people, "it's permitted" wouldn't end the conversation. A review seat exists to ask whether the exception is warranted, short enough, and mitigated. Stressed animals also make noisier data, so the facility has its own reason to care.

**Why not just the quiet word.** It's the kindest route, but it leaves no record that anyone examined the question. If Marcus adjusts, great, but nothing carries over to the next renovation. If he doesn't, you've spent your concern privately and your later silence reads as assent. Your vote or silence is part of the outcome either way.

**Why not formal only.** Marcus is your friend as well as the proposer. Surprising him in committee costs trust that doesn't need to be spent, and it makes him defensive when you want him to engage. Something like: *"When this comes to review I'm going to ask about the single-housing piece: justification, duration, mitigation. I'm not opposing the renovation, I just want it documented and as easy on the animals as it can be. Wanted you to hear it from me first."* That's honest, gives him time to prepare, and doesn't ask him to change anything before the process runs. Also tell the chair about the friendship. It's rarely disqualifying, and disclosing it protects you both.

**What to ask.** You don't know yet whether the plan already addresses these, so ask rather than assert:

- Is single housing necessary at all? Could the work be phased, or pairs moved *together* to other space or another site? The renovation and the separation are separable, and the plan may have fused them.
- If separation is unavoidable, can partners keep protected or grooming contact through panels or mesh? That preserves tactile contact and substantially helps re-pairing. At minimum, can they keep visual and auditory contact?
- What are the enrichment and behavioral monitoring plans, with defined endpoints for intervening on an individual animal?
- Is there a written reintroduction protocol involving behavioral staff, and a plan for pairs that fail?
- Is the four months firm, and what happens when construction overruns, as it often does? Is there a check-in point that triggers re-review?
- Has the attending veterinarian weighed in?

Framed this way, you're not obstructing Marcus. You're helping build a plan that holds up if something goes wrong, which protects him too. If the answers are already good, the questions cost five minutes and the record shows the committee looked. If they aren't, the gaps are where the animals' welfare can improve.

The risk is that Marcus bristles, and you may feel some friction. But a friendship that can't survive "justify this and document the mitigation" was already fragile, and the other costs of silence, to the animals and to what your seat means, are larger. I can draft the heads-up message or the written concern if you'd like.
